consensus_summary: Primary meaning is Jesus Christ as the innocent sacrificial Lamb of God who atones for sin (fusing Passover, Levitical sacrifice, and Isaiah 53), with settled consensus across traditions; common alternatives include the conquering Lamb of Revelation, believers as vulnerable lambs/sheep of the flock, and general meekness/innocence.
book_summary: Lamb means one of the flock—a covenant person—not by itself Christ (examples: Nathan’s ewe lamb, Jeremiah, disciples as lambs among wolves); the Lamb of God is specifically Christ, the perfect unblemished lamb taken out from the sheep.
consensus_core_identification: Jesus Christ as the sacrificial Lamb of God
book_core_identification: a covenant person / one of the flock (Christ only as the special perfect Lamb of God taken out from the sheep)
boundary_disagreement: Book excludes plain “lamb” from Christ (explicitly “not by itself Christ”) and restricts the christological sense to the qualified title “Lamb of God” as perfect member of the flock category; consensus treats “Lamb” (especially as title) as primarily and independently Christ while listing flock-members only as secondary alternative.
material_contradiction: Book’s assertion that the lamb is “not by itself Christ” directly negates the consensus’s settled primary identification of the Lamb as Christ the atoning sacrifice; the two cores cannot both be true as the default referent of the same term.
rationale: Minimum cores conflict: consensus centers the symbol on Christ (with people-as-lambs as alternative), while the book centers it on ordinary covenant flock-members and reclassifies Christ only as a qualified special case drawn out of that category. This replaces rather than merely narrows or conditions the consensus referent. Shared secondary cases (believers; “Lamb of God”) do not erase the contradiction at the primary identification; accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus primary.
strongest_objection: NT usage (John 1:29/36, Revelation’s Lamb, 1 Cor 5:7, 1 Pet 1:19) and historic Christian consensus establish Christ as the primary settled meaning of the Lamb, with flock-member uses secondary; the book’s inversion and “not by itself Christ” claim lacks decisive warrant from the listed verses alone.
